name: Mucuna pruriens

card.summary: A tropical bean rich in natural L-DOPA, used in Ayurveda and sold as a dopamine, libido and testosterone supplement; human evidence exists mainly for Parkinson's disease.
card.note: Contains L-DOPA; nausea and vomiting are reported at higher intakes and MAO inhibitor users are advised to avoid it. Pod hairs cause severe itching.

quick.overview:
Mucuna pruriens is a climbing legume whose seeds contain roughly 3 to 6 percent L-DOPA, the precursor to dopamine. Ayurvedic tradition uses the seeds as a nerve tonic and aphrodisiac, and the powder is sold as a supplement for mood, motivation, libido and male fertility.

The human evidence is mainly in Parkinson's disease: a small crossover study of 8 patients found seed powder gave faster onset and longer on-time than standard levodopa/carbidopa. No human trial for appearance-related use was found; fertility and testosterone claims rest on animal studies.
quick.mechanism: L-DOPA is converted to dopamine by the enzyme aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase. Forum users discuss pairing it with other supplements to modify this pathway; in Parkinson's treatment, levodopa is combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor because much converts to dopamine outside the brain.
quick.risks: L-DOPA sensitivity can cause nausea, vomiting, cramping, arrhythmias and low blood pressure, according to Wikipedia, which advises people on MAOIs to avoid the plant. A looksmax.org user reported vomiting after taking many capsules. Contact with raw pod hairs causes severe itching.

lead: Mucuna pruriens, the velvet bean, is a tropical climbing legume native to Africa and tropical Asia, grown as forage and green manure and eaten in parts of Indonesia [1]. Its seeds contain about 3 to 6 percent L-DOPA (levodopa), the dopamine precursor used in Parkinson's disease treatment, while its pod hairs contain compounds that cause intense itching [1].

Traditional Indian and African medicine uses the seeds as an aphrodisiac, nervine tonic and remedy for male infertility and Parkinsonian conditions [2]. In looksmaxxing and biohacking forums it is discussed as a source of dopamine, motivation and libido [3][4]. A small randomized crossover trial in Parkinson's disease reported that seed powder acted faster and gave longer on-time than standard levodopa/carbidopa [5]. No published human trial of its use for appearance, testosterone or fertility was found among the sources reviewed; related findings come from animal studies [6].

paras: Agricultural uses include forage, fallow and green-manure crops, and the beans are fermented into a tempeh-like food in Java [1]. In traditional medicine the seeds are used for male infertility, nervous disorders, Parkinson's disease, diabetes and rheumatism [2]. Supplements sell seed powder or L-DOPA-standardized extract.

A 2004 randomized, controlled, double-blind crossover study gave eight patients with Parkinson's disease single doses of levodopa/carbidopa and two doses of mucuna seed powder. The higher dose gave a faster onset and about 37 minutes (21.9 percent) longer on-time, with higher peak plasma levodopa, and no significant difference in dyskinesias; the authors called for a larger long-term trial [5]. ClinicalTrials.gov lists a phase 2 trial of mucuna therapy in Parkinson's disease with 18 participants [7].

Studies of mucuna in fertility and testosterone have been done in animals: rat studies reported improved sperm parameters and testis histology, and a rabbit study reported shorter mounting latency and improved semen measures [6]. These are not human data. The sources reviewed contain no human randomized trial of mucuna for libido, testosterone or appearance outcomes.

Wikipedia reports that people sensitive to L-DOPA may experience nausea, vomiting, cramping, arrhythmias and hypotension, and advises that people taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors avoid the plant because of seed tryptamines [1]. Grokipedia lists nausea, insomnia, bloating, hallucinations or psychosis at high or prolonged intake [2]. A looksmax.org user reported vomiting about 90 to 120 minutes after taking a large number of capsules [3]. The pod hairs cause dermatitis and severe itch, and mucuna is used in experimental itch models in human volunteers [1][8].

L-DOPA is decarboxylated to dopamine by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase; in conventional Parkinson's therapy a peripheral inhibitor such as carbidopa is added because dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier [4][5]. Seeds also contain serotonin and tryptamines [1].
On looksmax.org, threads discuss mucuna as an over-the-counter dopamine source and combine it with other supplements aimed at slowing dopamine breakdown [4].

timeline.event: Species described under its binomial name [1]
Crossover trial in 8 Parkinson's patients compares seed powder with levodopa/carbidopa [5]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org mucuna is discussed as an over-the-counter dopamine and drive supplement, and users share self-experiments including reports of side effects [3][4].

claims.claim: Mucuna pruriens is a way to "dopamine max" because it contains L-DOPA
claims.believers: Forum proponents note that it contains the dopamine precursor L-DOPA and can be bought without a prescription, and discuss stacking it with green tea extract and quercetin to slow dopamine breakdown [4].
claims.experts: Mucuna seed powder has been tested against levodopa/carbidopa in a small Parkinson's study, where it raised plasma levodopa; no published human study has tested it as a mood, drive or appearance supplement [5].

claims.believers: One user posted a self-experiment reporting vomiting roughly 90 to 120 minutes after taking many capsules [3].
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists nausea and vomiting among effects in people sensitive to L-DOPA [1].

claims.claim: Mucuna boosts libido and male fertility
claims.believers: Proponents cite traditional Ayurvedic use as an aphrodisiac and fertility tonic [2].
claims.experts: Animal studies report improved sperm and testis measures; no human randomized trial was found among the sources reviewed [6].
